title: Stock Management System
description: Full-stack serial-level inventory ledger with a units-as-source-of-truth data model, derived quantities, an audit trail, and Word-template warranty generation
tech_stack: React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, TanStack Query, Node.js, Express, Prisma, PostgreSQL, Vitest
detail_description: A full-stack internal inventory system that tracks commercial-display stock down to the individual serial number: what is physically owned, what is in the warehouse, and where each unit was shipped. Built as a ground-up rebuild of an earlier spreadsheet system. Each physical unit is a single database row, and all quantities (in-stock, shipped, in-transit) are derived by counting rows rather than stored as hand-edited counters. Includes product/unit CRUD with status-aware corrections, a derived invoices view, an append-only audit log, and a warranty module that fills a real .docx template. React + Vite frontend with typed API hooks, an Express + Prisma + PostgreSQL backend, and a pure, unit-tested domain layer (80 domain + 35 integration tests).
challenges: The previous system stored quantity counters that drifted out of sync with reality, so the numbers could not be trusted — the same model could show a stock count that disagreed with the actual units on hand. Real exported data was also messy: duplicate and corrupted serials, placeholder values, and legacy records entered by someone else.
solution: Redesigned around a units-as-source-of-truth model: quantities are derived from unit rows via a Postgres view, and invariants (unique real serials, non-negative owned, in-stock <= owned) are enforced with database constraints and partial-unique indexes so bad data cannot enter. Business rules live in a pure, tested domain layer; thin Express routes call it inside transactions and write an audit record for every change. Chose a .docx-fill approach for warranty documents over server-side PDF rendering because the cPanel deploy target could not run the required engines.
outcome: A trustworthy per-serial inventory ledger where quantities can no longer silently drift, every change is auditable and reversible, and warranty documents generate straight from the real company template — acting as an independent check against the accounting system at year end.

title: Finding Pattern in Chaos: Powerball Audit
description: Statistical audit of 444 Australian Powerball draws: 28 tests, 5,000 simulated fair lotteries and a trained model, to see whether any pattern beats chance
tech_stack: Python, Pandas, NumPy, Statistical Testing, Monte Carlo Simulation, Logistic Regression, Matplotlib, Jupyter
detail_description: An independent, recreational research project that asks whether the history of Australian Powerball (444 weekly draws of the current 7-from-35 format, 2018 to 2026) hides any exploitable pattern. It derives the exact odds, reviews the gambler's and hot-hand fallacy literature and critiques a preprint that claims to predict lottery numbers, then runs a 28-test scorecard against 5,000 simulated fair lotteries, five walk-forward prediction strategies, and a light trained model. Results are published as a paper, a poster and an interactive site.
challenges: Hunting through hundreds of statistics will always throw up something that looks significant, so the hard part was separating luck from signal. Many statistics (maxima, droughts, streaks) have no closed-form distribution. Any pattern found after looking at the data cannot be trusted, and a model can look good on the data it was fitted to. A pipeline bug would look the same as a null result.
solution: Used exact hypergeometric and geometric formulas wherever they exist and simulated 5,000 fair lotteries (fixed seed) for everything else. Fixed a 28-test scorecard up front and judged it with Bonferroni and Benjamini-Hochberg corrections and a p-value histogram. Calibrated the method by planting known defects in synthetic lotteries. Tested prediction strategies walk-forward with a random control, and trained a nine-parameter logistic model with a chronological hold-out and a 100-lottery placebo. Wrote a 26-check script that re-implements the pipeline independently, including a no-look-ahead test and a full enumeration of all 6,724,520 tickets.
outcome: No evidence of bias: none of the 28 tests survived correction (smallest p = 0.084), five prediction strategies performed no better than a random pick, and the trained model matched random tickets on the 89 newest held-out draws. Most interesting findings: any rule that excludes combinations leaves the unconditional odds of winning exactly unchanged; the model fitted more structure to older draws than any of 100 fair lotteries yet it vanished out of sample; and two post-hoc hints (a lag-6 echo and decade bunching) are kept as hypotheses for a prospective test on future draws.
